passage: The school bus dropped Trisha at the edge of the village at four, dusty and silent. Her father Anand looked up from mending the fence. 'How was the test? Did Ma'am return your notebook? Who won at kho-kho?' Trisha dropped her bag. 'Nothing.' Then, sharply, 'Leave me!' Anand opened his mouth to scold, then remembered his own long schooldays. He handed her a guava from the tree and said only, 'The goats need taking to the pond.' Trisha walked them down alone and threw pebbles into the water for a long time. At dinner she told him everything, even the kho-kho score.

qa.q: What did Anand hand Trisha?
qa.a: A guava from the tree.

qa.q: What does Trisha's sharp 'Leave me!' suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: She was drained and irritable after a long school day and needed space before any questions.

qa.q: What made Anand's second response better than his first?
qa.a: Instead of more questions or a scolding, he offered a snack and time alone with the goats, so she could recover and chose to talk later.

qa.q: What was it like for Anand when Trisha snapped at him?
qa.a: He was tempted to scold but remembered his own schooldays, and was rewarded when she told him everything at dinner.

grounding: Shows a schoolchild silent and irritable after a long day who needs a snack and time alone before talking, and later opens up.

passage: Jana's key turned in the door of the apartment in Oslo at half past three. She kicked off her boots, walked past her father Lars without a word, and shut herself in her room. Lars had a list of questions ready: the spelling test, the class trip form, her friend's birthday. He looked at the closed door and put the list away. Instead he cut an apple, spread a little peanut butter on the slices, and left the plate outside her door with a knock. For half an hour there was only the sound of building blocks clicking together. Then Jana came out, plate empty, and leaned on the kitchen counter. 'Pappa, guess what happened at recess.'

qa.q: What did Lars leave outside Jana's door?
qa.a: A plate of apple slices with a little peanut butter.

qa.q: What might Jana have been feeling when she walked past Lars without a word?
qa.a: She was probably tired and overloaded after a long school day and wanted to be alone before talking.

qa.q: What could other parents learn from Lars's choice?
qa.a: Holding back the questions and offering a snack and quiet play time lets a child recover, and often they start talking on their own.

qa.q: If you were Lars looking at the closed door, what would you be tempted to do?
qa.a: You might want to knock and ask all the questions at once, or feel shut out, but waiting gave Jana room and brought her back chatting.

grounding: Shows a schoolchild silent after a long day who needs time alone and a snack before talking, and a parent who finds that works better than immediate questions.

passage:
'Yusuf, how was the test? What did Ma'am say? Show me your diary.'
'Abbu, I don't know.'
'What do you mean you don't know? Pankaj Sir is coming at five for tuition.'
'Leave me!' Yusuf threw his bag down and stomped to the bed.
Ammi put a plate of poha and a banana on the table. 'Let him eat first. He's been in that noise since seven.'
'But the homework...'
'Half an hour. Let him kick his ball in the lane.'
At half past four Yusuf came back sweaty and smiling. 'Abbu, guess what? I got nine out of ten!'

qa.q: What did Ammi put on the table?
qa.a: A plate of poha and a banana.

qa.q: Why did Yusuf shout 'Leave me!'?
qa.a: He was drained and irritable after a long, noisy school day, and the rush of questions felt like too much.

qa.q: What approach worked better than questioning Yusuf straight away?
qa.a: A snack and half an hour kicking his ball gave him time to recover, and then he shared his news himself.

qa.q: How might Abbu have felt when Yusuf threw his bag?
qa.a: Abbu probably felt hurt and frustrated, since he only wanted to hear about the test.

grounding: A schoolchild snaps when questioned after a long day, and a snack and free play first bring back his good mood.

passage: When I come home from school, my ears are still ringing. Forty-two kids, a bell every forty minutes, and the bus horn all the way. Last month Mummy asked me questions at the door and I went silent and slammed my room door. My little brother Yogesh would jump on me to play, and I yelled at him. Then Mummy started something new. Now she just says, 'Hi, Pradeep,' hands me a banana and leaves me alone. I lie on the floor and build with my blocks for a while. After that I actually want to tell her about my day, and I even let Yogesh help me build.

qa.q: What does Mummy hand Pradeep now?
qa.a: A banana.

qa.q: How did Pradeep feel coming home from school last month?
qa.a: Pradeep felt drained and irritable with ears still ringing, so questions at the door led to silence and a slammed door.

qa.q: What new approach did Mummy try?
qa.a: She greets Pradeep, hands over a banana and allows time alone with the blocks before any talking.

qa.q: What was it like for Yogesh when Pradeep yelled?
qa.a: Yogesh probably felt hurt and confused, since he only wanted to play.

grounding: A child worn out by a noisy school day needs a snack and time alone before talking.

passage:
After-school centre notes, Thursday
Indu arrived at 3:30 looking pale and tight-lipped, and when Farzana asked her to join the quiz she burst into tears and hid under the reading table. I did not ask what was wrong. I left a cup of water and some peanut chikki beside her and let her be. After twenty minutes she came out and began building a tower of blocks alone. At 4:30 she wandered over and told me, unprompted, that her class had practised for sports day in the sun all afternoon. From now on: Indu gets a snack and free play first, and homework starts at 4:30.
Kishore

qa.q: Where did Indu hide?
qa.a: Under the reading table.

qa.q: What might Indu have been feeling when she burst into tears over the quiz?
qa.a: She was exhausted and overwhelmed after practising in the sun all afternoon, with nothing left for a quiz.

qa.q: What did Kishore decide for Indu from now on?
qa.a: A snack and free play first, with homework starting at 4:30.

qa.q: How might Farzana have felt when Indu cried at the quiz invitation?
qa.a: Farzana may have felt confused or a little hurt, not knowing Indu simply needed rest.

grounding: A carer notes that a tired child needs a snack and time alone after school before activities and talk.

passage:
Thursday
School was so LOUD today. Assembly, then a test, then PT in the sun, then the bus with everyone screaming songs. When I got home Pallavi didi asked "How was school? What did you get in the test? Did you give the form?" all at once, and I shouted "LEAVE ME!" and went under the table. Then I felt bad. Mummy didn't ask anything. She put a plate of poha and a banana next to the table and went away. I ate it and played with my marbles for a long time. After that I wanted to talk. I told didi about the test (8 out of 10!) and said sorry. Then I did homework.
Ramesh

qa.q: What did Mummy put next to the table?
qa.a: A plate of poha and a banana.

qa.q: Why did Ramesh shout "LEAVE ME!" at Pallavi didi?
qa.a: Ramesh was worn out and irritable after a long, loud day, and too many questions at once felt overwhelming.

qa.q: Why did Mummy's approach work better than questions?
qa.a: A snack and quiet play gave Ramesh time alone to recover, and after that Ramesh wanted to talk.

qa.q: How might Pallavi didi have felt when Ramesh shouted?
qa.a: She was probably hurt and surprised, since she was only curious about the day.

grounding: Shows a schoolchild worn out by a noisy day needing time alone before talking and homework, with a snack and unstructured play working better than questions.
